p: And then how do you think the city can improve its disability information resources across all agencies?

Yeah. So, I think there’s a lot of priorities that can be done. Standardizing accessibility pages, plain language, and accessible forms, citywide accessible dashboard would be great, but again, I’m reviewing all these great suggestions that MOPD staff shared and others have shared, and I– once I do that, I would love to talk to staff and others on that.
Wonderful. I would like to turn it over to Finance Chair, Council Member Lee.
Thank you so much, Chair, and it’s so great to see you, Commissioner Agarwal.
It’s so good to see you.

Going back to when you were Commissioner at MOIA and I was at my nonprofit before, it is so great to see you, and thank you for always being a champion for us. My name is Linda Lee. I have dark brown hair. I’m wearing a black jacket, blue blouse. I have really dark circles under my eyes right now because it’s budget season. So, yes, and I’m Korean-American. So, for folks– and I’ve always argued that we should be giving you guys more funding when I was chair. And by the way, I just want to acknowledge the fact that I think it’s great that we have a completely separate Disabilities Committee and we have an amazing Chair is going to be helping to champion this. But as we know, a lot of our issues in the disabilities community impact every aspect of our city government. And so I’m super, super excited that this committee was able to be separated out and

get its due recognition and attention to be quite honest. So, just wanted to ask a little bit about the Preliminary Budget. I’ll be quick. In the FY 27 Preliminary Plan, MOPD has a Fiscal 2027 budgeted headcount of six positions. And so how are you– first of all, and I’d like to talk about where you think the needs need to grow, because I always felt like the budget for MOPD was extremely low considering the number of people you have to service in the city. And so out of the six budgeted positions, I believe three are vacant, or is it–
So, it actually is four headcount, and two position are unfunded.
Where’s it funded from, then? How is it?
I’ll explain.
Okay.

So, the four titles are Commissioner, Executive Assistant, Chief of Staff, and Assistant Commissioner. The two unfunded positioned were PEG’d in Fiscal Year 25, the November Plan. And however, we have staff of 20 people. Of the four, our position from the Office of

the Mayor. The remaining staff lines are four disability experts who are working on agency– parter agencies, but work indirectly with the coordination of MOPD. So, I’ll give you an example. I just talked about, At Work. At Work has six employees, and the partner agency is SBS. So, this cross-agency model actually allows disability experts to be embedded in MOPD, and it is a model that expands our impact without duplicating costs. So, it’s actually pretty– a good model.
I was going to say, so does that mean that there’s shared costs not just in staffing, but also in the other operational administrative costs as well?
Yes.

Okay, good to know, and thank you for that clarification. And I’m assuming that you’ve received the same letter of instructions asking agencies to look at different efficiencies, and is it– for you all at MOPD, is it the same percentage that you guys have to abide by with the 1.5–
[interposing] No.

No, it’s not, right? Okay. Just wanted to make sure. And actually, the other questions I’ll forgo just because you answered it with the staffing part. So, thank you. And just I know that the Chair is going to be asking more questions, but it would be great if you can inform us on– you know, and I see through your testimony, inform of us on some of your new needs and areas where you want to see growth. So thank you.
Will do.
Thank you, Chair.

Alright, wonderful. So, in Fiscal 2026, November Plan, $25,000 in other categorical funding was added to MOPD’s budget for handicapped parking education, and only with an additional budgeted headcount of one. Could you explain specifically what this funding is going to be used for and why it’s added as a one-time funding, and what’s the title of the additional position associated, and has this position been hired yet?

Yeah. So, the one-time funding comes from revenue collected through summons issued to individuals who wrongly parked in

the spaces designated for people with disabilities, and this funding is OTPS, so there is no additional funding asked. It’s just a one-time $25,000. And I am planning for this funding for my new mission and vision, and so I’m thinking through that as well.
Got it. And did this exist in the past as well?
It has. So, we frequently receive this money when people decide to put their cars in other than the spaces that are designated for people with disabilities. So, it fluctuates.
Got it. And is Fiscal 26 budget higher than the previous fiscal year?
I don’t know. Do you know?
And I know it’s contingent on somebody getting ticketed.

Yeah, right, right. So, the revenues come from the summons issued by NYPD, and then the funds are transferred from DOF

to Mayor’s Office. And this fiscal year’s revenue was $25,000. It’s actually lower than before, only because we’ve been effective at ad campaigns for stopping people from parking in spaces that are designated for people with disabilities. So, there’s less summons which means less revenue.

Got it. And then this program, this education program, is this a signature workshop that you all provide? What is it, and can it– if you have zero dollars, let’s say nobody’s received a summons, this program can exist without that?
Well, if people– if that is zero, that would be fantastic, and we do trainings and education material on various topics including this. So, that would be consistent on our work.
And could you just describe what the handicapped parking education looks like?
The– it’s not an education thing. It’s just called Handicap Parking Education.
The funding that comes from the summons.
Oh yeah. Okay. Hold one. Why don’t you share?
I’m talking about if that funding is being used for this program–
[interposing] Yeah, so–
[interposing] but you can clarify if I’m not–

[interposing] Yeah, just to clarify, I think Commissioner Agarawal had mentioned that this was a one-time OTPS funding that comes through MOPD on an annual basis, only because it’s contingent on the number of summonses issued. It historically is used– the funding that came was used to then advertise to the community about not parking in spaces designated for people with disabilities.
Got it. So, this funding is specifically related still to the parking issue.
Yes.
Okay, understood.
And my apologies.
No, no worries. And has this position been hired?
There’s no–
[interposing] There’s no position.
Yes.
So, this is just a one-shot deal for parking education. Okay. So, the Preliminary Plan lists one contract in MOPD’s budget for roughly $16,000 in FY 27. Could you share the details of this contract?
Yeah. So, this money is designated to ASL interpreters, and that’s the primary, and then we have– that’s about $16,000, and then we have another $7,000
That’s within the $16K or in addition?
Yes.
Okay. And is the contractor a provider from New York City, or is it in-house?
Yeah, the contractor Sign Nexus.
Do you mind spelling that? And do you provide– or do they provide tactile interpretation as well?
I assume they do, but we can double check. And the– it’s S-i-g-n, Sign, Nexus, N–e-x-u-s.
And is this a vendor that the city has been using consistently?
Yes.
And do you all evaluate them or do you hear feedback from New Yorkers?
Yeah. So, advocates and members of the MOPD actually like working with Sign Nexus. So, we haven’t received any complaints about them.
What percentage of MOPD and DOHMH contracts go to disability-led organizations?
We don’t provide like contracting services.
So, you don’t serve as like a conduit or as a grant or–
[interposing] Yeah, exactly.
And then, are MWBE and disability-owned businesses prioritized in city procurement?
Yes. And we work with the city of– the Mayor’s Office to procure that.
And are you able to share how many vendors that are disability-owned or providing services to New York City?
We can’t now, but we will find out and share it with you later.
Yeah, I’d really love to know. I mean, this is– it’s critical that we’re not only just talking about access, but we’re also empowering people with disabilities to be entrepreneurs.

And I think one of– yeah. And one of the highlights that I mentioned in the testimony is our work on At Work, and that

impacts people with disabilities to get employment, and that’s been very successful in the past, and something that I hope it will be able to grow.

Moving on to other budget needs. Following the conclusion of FY 27 hearings, the Council will release its Preliminary Budget response where we will outline budget priority items which would be included in future financial plans. What are MOPD’s most pressing budget needs?
Again, we will talk to City Hall and OMB in this discussion.
You’re not able to say what might be the priorities? You have to–
[interposing] I mean, we’re– I’m restructuring and so we don’t have ideas at the moment, but I’m working with City Hall and OMB. The goal is to create a new structure.
Got it. And then at the moment, how many more budget positions does MOPD need?
For now, we don’t have that request, but we’ll let you know if that changes.
So, there are no other staff lines that are vacant?
We have one line that’s vacant, and I’m interviewing those people.

Okay, got it. Coming back to the workforce. As a disabled city worker who has required accommodations in my own work place, I want to turn to questions about disabled city workers. What percentage of the city workforce identifies as having a disability?

That– so, I can say– people in the workforce. I have figured that out. Let me see. The headcount, we had shared that there are– hold on. Give me one second. In the– we have 40 percent of New Yorkers with disabilities of working age are employed. So, figuring that math out really rapidly, it would be say a million, 40 percent of a million if that makes sense.
Well, I’m not good at math.
I know, I’m really bad at math, too. We can tell you later and– if that helps.
And does MOPD provide additional support for those who want to get a city job?

Absolutely, and that’s the reason At Work, New York City At Work is– helps individually people who are seeking jobs and people who are employers, and they connect that in place. And so, I find that the work done of New York City At Work is successfully– is successful, and it could grow as well. And it has been done so well. And then– yeah.
I would still love to get the math–
[interposing] Yeah.
of the amount of city workers who identify as having a disability, and you know, I want to make sure that New Yorkers feel empowered.
Yep.
That they don’t just have to apply for positions that relate to addressing disabilities in New York City.
Yes, for sure.
And so how are we recruiting and retaining, and are there plans for promotions and advancements in their roles?

And I’m going to meet with the Commissioner of DCAS, because she runs, or they run 55A program that helps people with disabilities to get jobs without having to go through the examination process. And currently, we have about half. It’s like 700 jobs by people with disabilities, but only half are filled, and so we want to talk to the Commissioner of ways that we can address that or– and ensure that more people with disabilities get jobs.
Could you just repeat that one more time? 700 people–
[interposing] There’s 700 people– job slots, and only half are filled by people with disabilities.
Got it. What accommodations exist for city employees, and how quickly are they provided?

Yeah. So, broadly, every agency has ADA requirements, EEO staff involved, and so using that– like, when I was in the Health Department, I knew that if I had any problems related to my disability, I could talk to people in EEO. We also had DSF people engaged on that topic, and so we have the people in staff. It’s how do we create jobs that transition, that new jobs or existing jobs to people with disabilities to ensure that the job that they’re most excited for that can get access to that.
And then, you know, during COVID or the thick of COVID, there was a campaign by city workers to be able to work remote or have a remote accommodation that is written into our policy.
Yeah.

And the administration did not support that, and that really created harm for many, many families who had been either taking care of a loved one with long COVID or were still getting sick, did not want to come into the office as a result of that, and other issues. Do

you believe that we should have a remote work option that’s not just negotiated between the director and the staff person?

I mean, I– I can’t speak in general, but I think it’s like for MOPD we have hybrid work environments. So, people when they'll come to the office we have a list of that and when they’re going to stay home. And I think that works fine. Also, I think that based on the agency, based on the company, it varies in case to case. I can’t say in full that I like remote, because I just don’t know about every job that’s happening.

Again, during COVID, MOPD partnered with DCAS and H+H to distribute 10,000 at-home test kits designed specifically for people who are vision impaired. For recent emergencies like snowstorms and hurricanes, what other work has MOPD done to help the disability community receive necessary services or supplies?

Yeah. Yeah. So, MOPD works closely with NYCEM, the NYC Emergency Management, to ensure disabled New Yorkers are integral on emergency planning. So, we do accessible

alerts and the communications planning for accessibility evacuation centers and shelters. We participate in emergency work activity meetings, and ensure ISL, captions, and plain language are available on emergency alerts, among others.
Could you talk a little bit more about the accessible evaluation centers, I think you mentioned?

Yeah. So, there’s– I have not been to one yet, but I think they are regularly are involved in many agencies getting together about– for example, snow removal– and that is an area that MOPD is also engaged in that topic. We share the impact that that may have with people with disabilities.
Now, do you all lean on NYCEM for the supplies and resources, or are you informing what supplies and resources they should be procuring?

Yeah, so it’s really a coordination effort. So, if we think about COVID and the accessible test kits, we worked with MOPD, H+H and DCAS to create these kits, and MOPD

were identifying organizations across the city, including independent living centers, providers with blind or low-vision priorities, etcetera. DCAS did the logistics and provided support on that when MOPD coordinated the other organizations to use the kits and to deliver it to people who are blind and low-vision New Yorkers. So, the idea is coordination with other city agencies, moving that forward.
Got it. So, as I’m understanding it, MOPD is bringing together the disability-led organizations, assisted living centers, etcetera and getting them the resources.
Yes, exactly.
And is there an evaluation process, or do you hear from these groups about what more they could use or how has the response been during emergencies?

Yeah. First of all, I wasn’t involved in MOPD at the time, but the numbers are outstanding. So, we– they secured 175,000 masks and 170 gloves to 64 disability-serving organizations, and directly to 6,500 individuals. We also facilitated a donation of 25,000 masks for D73.

And so all the stuff we do, I think that what I’ve learned for the last three weeks is that MOPD does a lot and they don’t get enough credit, and they’re so engaged and able to do these things, and so I think that’s very important to note.
And then with the disability groups, are you all meeting with them regularly? What is the relationship beyond providing [inaudible].

Yeah. So, in the past, they did quarterly community calls, and I can go into the details on that, but from my perspective we should meet constantly and not just quarterly. And so we are having a meeting in the next week or two, a group of community members and partnering with them. It is actually key to me on how we can work with MOPD and the communities that are affected.
And is the budget that you all have enough for expanding the engagement with the organizations you work with? So the money that you already have allotted is–
[interposing] Yeah.
going to be used for that work.
Yes.
Even though you are going to expand engagement with them?
Yes, exactly.
Coming back to At Work, how many workers have been– New Yorkers with disabilities been connected to jobs or internships through At Work?

Yeah. So between July 2023 and June 2025, the program provided services to 130 people with disabilities and helped 99 individuals obtain employment. And then the program also hosted 62 workshops for job-seekers and community members, participated in 200– 20– my number is like aphasia– 200 mock interviews, and hosted seven job trainings. And then citywide, New York City Talent did 373 individuals with disability connection in 24 to 25. And I apologize. It’s my aphasia, so if I have– I can share the numbers that are accurate if you– if that’s helpful.
Absolutely. Thank you. Are those numbers, were they goals? Did you all have a plan in terms of like here’s how many people want to reach and reach them and delivered?
Yeah, so in the last administration I think the goal was 2,500 and we surpassed that by much more, and so that's been really–
[interposing] That’s to provide trainings or who received jobs?
Training and received jobs. Right? Yeah.
So, 2,500 people with disabilities were employed?

Yes. In the last administration the goal was to connect 2,500 job-seekers with disabilities connected to jobs, and as of this year– the three-year anniversary of that program is this July, but we’ve so far surpassed that goal. We’re at 3,737 individuals that have been connected to jobs, but this number is in partnership to MOPD and SBS and NYC Talent and DCAS.
Got it. And do you all know if that number still remains? Are folks still in their positions?

We can get that information to you. There is a team that analyzes the retention services of the individuals who have been connected. So, after this hearing, we can get you the numbers of how many people have still– are in those positions.
Yeah. It would be good to know about the retention around this program. And could you also just share what the budget for NYC At Work is, this cycle and the last fiscal cycle?
So, in 2024 and 2025 it was $543,000, and then 2026 and 2027 is $584,000, approximately.
Okay, a little bit of a bump.
Yeah.
